summary: This informational document describes RADIUS vendor-specific attributes defined by the DSL Forum. They carry DSL information the standard attribute set cannot, and serve as a reference so DSL equipment vendors can interoperate. It is expected to be updated if more attributes are defined.

plainLanguage.summary: DSL gear needs to pass along special notes that the normal RADIUS form has no box for. This lists the extra boxes the DSL industry group invented so every maker fills them in the same way.

questions: what are dsl forum radius vsa
how do radius vendor specific attributes work
subtitle: Extra fields for RADIUS to carry DSL-specific information that standard attributes cannot hold.

tldr.problem: RADIUS is the standard protocol for authentication and accounting in broadband networks, but it was not designed with DSL-specific data in mind. DSL line characteristics like actual speed, line identification, and performance limits have no home in the original RADIUS attributes.
tldr.mechanism: The DSL Forum defined vendor-specific RADIUS attributes (VSAs) using RADIUS's extension mechanism. These attributes carry DSL line identification, data rates, delay information, and access loop configuration so DSL equipment vendors can interoperate.
tldr.outcome: DSL operators and equipment makers can now include detailed line information in authentication and accounting messages using a standard vendor-specific format, enabling better service management.

today: RFC 4679 is an Informational document from September 2006 and has not been updated or obsoleted. It remains the canonical reference for DSL Forum RADIUS VSAs and continues to be used by DSL operators and equipment vendors for interoperability, although the specification note indicates the document may be updated if the DSL Forum defines additional attributes.

sections.title: The Need for DSL-Specific Attributes
sections.content:
RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) is the standard protocol for authenticating and accounting for broadband connections. When a subscriber dials in or starts a session, RADIUS servers decide whether to allow the connection and log what happened.

But RADIUS was designed in the 1990s for generic dial-up scenarios. Modern DSL networks have much richer information to track: which physical DSL port a subscriber is connected to, how fast their line actually is, what the speed limits are, and how much delay the signal experiences. The standard RADIUS attributes have no place for this DSL-specific data.

Rather than inventing a completely new protocol, the DSL Forum used Vendor-Specific Attributes (VSAs)—an extension mechanism built into RADIUS—to define a standardized set of DSL attributes that all vendors can use consistently.
sections.plainLanguage: RADIUS is the checklist for letting people on the network. But it did not have blanks for "which DSL port" or "how fast is this line." The DSL industry made official extra boxes so everyone writes the same information the same way.

sections.title: How VSAs Work
sections.content:
A RADIUS Vendor-Specific Attribute is a container that holds vendor-defined sub-attributes. The VSA itself has a standard RADIUS type (26), a length field, and a Vendor ID (3561 for the DSL Forum).

Inside the container are sub-attributes: each has a Vendor-Type (a single byte identifying which sub-attribute it is), a Vendor-Length, and a Value. The value can be a string (like a subscriber identifier) or an integer (like a data rate in bits per second).

This nesting allows vendors to extend RADIUS without breaking older equipment. Devices that do not recognize a particular vendor-specific sub-attribute simply ignore it, while newer devices can process the new information.
sections.plainLanguage: A vendor-specific attribute is like a mailing envelope inside the RADIUS package. Inside the envelope are labeled sub-envelopes, each with its own data. Old RADIUS systems throw away the whole envelope; new ones open it and read the labels.

sections.title: Identifying and Describing the Subscriber Line
sections.content:
Two key VSAs identify the DSL connection itself. The Agent-Circuit-Id identifies the physical DSL port on the Access Node or DSLAM (Digital Subscriber Line Access Multiplexer) where the subscriber is connected. It is typically a string like "slot 3, port 0" or might include an ATM virtual circuit identifier (VPI.VCI) or Ethernet VLAN tag, depending on whether the line uses ATM or Ethernet.

The Agent-Remote-Id is an operator-defined string that identifies the subscriber on that line. It might be a billing account number, a telephone number, a network address, or any other value the service provider chooses. Unlike Agent-Circuit-Id, which is tied to the physical port, Agent-Remote-Id is whatever the operator configured to identify that specific customer.
sections.plainLanguage: Agent-Circuit-Id is like the street address where the phone line is ("the box in the basement, slot 3, jack 5"). Agent-Remote-Id is like the customer name or account number that goes into that jack.

sections.title: Speed and Performance Characteristics
sections.content:
The VSA set includes multiple attributes for different notions of data rate, all measured in bits per second:

Actual-Data-Rate attributes tell you the real-time upstream and downstream speeds that the modem synchronized with the line. These change as line conditions vary (noise, cross-talk, signal attenuation).

Minimum-Data-Rate attributes are the operator-configured floor: the slowest the line will ever be asked to run under normal conditions. If the actual rate drops below this minimum, the operator may disable the line.

Attainable-Data-Rate attributes reflect what the DSLAM measured as the maximum speed the line could theoretically reach given its current conditions (loop length, noise floor, etc.). It is what the system targets for sync.

Maximum-Data-Rate attributes are the operator-set ceiling: the fastest the line is allowed to go, regardless of what it could achieve. Also included are special low-power versions of minimum rates for when the line drops into power-saving mode.

These rates are critical for service level agreements and troubleshooting.
sections.plainLanguage: An actual speed tells you how fast it runs right now. A minimum is the slowest the company will let it go. An attainable is the best it could do. A maximum is the fastest the company will allow. Lines can also drop into a low-power mode where they need less speed.

sections.title: Interleaving Delay and Access Loop Details
sections.content:
DSL systems add a delay buffer called interleaving to the data stream, trading some latency for better error correction on noisy lines. The Interleaving-Delay VSAs capture the maximum allowed interleaving delay (separately for upstream and downstream) and the actual delay in use.

The Access-Loop-Encapsulation attribute describes how the DSL signal is packaged at the line interface: it might specify ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) framing with specific Virtual Path and Virtual Circuit identifiers, or Ethernet framing with an optional VLAN tag. This tells the network core how to interpret the data arriving from the DSLAM.

The IWF-Session attribute marks sessions that are using an Interworking Function, a bridge that converts between PPPoA (PPP over ATM) and PPPoE (PPP over Ethernet), which is necessary when the subscriber's equipment speaks one protocol but the network uses the other.
sections.plainLanguage: Interleaving-Delay is how much we slow down the signal to fix errors better. Access-Loop-Encapsulation says whether the line uses ATM or Ethernet underneath. IWF-Session marks when we have to translate between two different signal types.
